column79: An initial breeding attempt progressed into early brooding but was classified as Abandoned based on a brief occurrence of recordings containing Begging Calls followed by a rapid decline in Tricolored Blackbird vocal detections. The only Begging Calls detected for this inital attempt were 2-6kHz Nestling Begging Calls. Because the higher 6-8 kHz Hatchling Begging Calls were never detected, an estimated brooding onset was calculated by subtracting 2 days from the first date that Nestling Begging Calls were detected, which is the typical time for Hatchling Begging Calls to develop into Nestling Begging Calls. Two additional breeding attempts occurred later in the season, each characterized by a complete sequence of recordings containing Nestling Begging Calls followed by Fledgling Begging Calls. The temporal spacing and partial overlap of these breeding attempts support classification of this colony as Complex. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for the latter two attempts, and each was therefore classified as Successful. The ARU deployed at this site was an LG cell phone, which produced lower-quality recordings than AudioMoth units and was prone to intermittent failure, resulting in gaps in recording coverage; while recording quality was sufficient for this analysis, direct comparisons to other datasets should be made with caution. The algorithm used to detetmine dispersal date selected a date in the middle of the weak stutter of Fledgling Begging Calls. The bulk of Fledglings left on 23 Jun, with intermittent detections of Fledgling Begging Calls continuing through the last day of recordings.

There were two ARUs deployed in this colony. This ARU had recordings from the most days and is considered the core dataset. Field visits documented a large colony that settled and initiated breeding at this site. Female Chatter detections were present initially but declined abruptly before estimated brooding onset. No Nestling or Fledgling Begging Call detections were recorded following this decline, supporting classification of the breeding attempt as Abandoned. The timing of Abandonment was temporally coincident with repeated helicopter noise detected acoustically at the site. Because no Begging Calls were detected, brooding onset was estimated as being sixteen days after Female Chatter was detected above the daily threshold, reflecting four days of nest building followed by twelve days of incubation prior to brooding onset. This difference is indicated in Table 5 with a "~".

The ARU deployed at this site was an LG cell phone, which produced lower-quality recordings than AudioMoth units and was prone to intermittent failure, resulting in gaps in recording coverage. Because Nestling Begging Calls are typically detected within two days of the onset of brooding; the presence of Female Chatter detections without corresponding Nestling Begging Call detections suggests that the breeding attempt was Partially Abandoned at the time of ARU failure. A period of prolonged extreme heat occurred immediately following brooding onset, including five consecutive days exceeding 95 °F and two days above 107 °F, and may have contributed to the outcome.

Although the timing of breeding stages varied slightly among the three deployments, stage transitions were generally consistent. This ARU was centrally located and was deployed shortly before the onset of brooding. No Male Chorus detections were recorded, indicating that chorus activity had likely ceased prior to deployment. Automated pattern matching performed well for the remaining vocalizations despite background noise from the nesting White-faced Ibis. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for approximately two weeks before dispersal, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful. Based on estimated brooding onset across all three ARUs, breeding activity appeared to initiate in the southern portion of the site and subsequently spread northward.

column79:
An initial synchronous breeding attempt was identified based on detections of Hatchling, Nestling, and Fledgling Begging Calls occurring in the expected temporal sequence. Targeted manual review for Hatchling Begging Calls during this first attempt identified three recordings on 17 May, followed by no detections on 18–19 May, coincident with a sharp increase in Male Chorus activity that likely masked these quieter vocalizations. As a result, Hatchling Begging Call detections did not meet the daily threshold for brooding onset. However, the detections on 17 May, together with the appearance of Begging Calls from older nestlings beginning on 20 May, support an estimated brooding onset of approximately 17 May. This date is therefore reported as approximate and is marked with a “~” in Table 5.

A second breeding attempt was also identified, occurring approximately 20 days after the first. Because Tricolored Blackbirds typically require at least 30 days between successive breeding attempts, this short interval indicates the arrival of an additional cohort rather than a repeat attempt by birds from the first cohort, resulting in overlapping breeding stages. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for both cohorts, and each attempt was therefore classified as Successful. Due to the close temporal overlap between the two attempts, dispersal for the first attempt and fledging onset for the second could not be assigned reliably.
column81: Sub-colony addition. After the first birds established a larger group appears to have joined them, resulting in overlapping breeding stages. So dates marked as nestling call not present when there is the loud male chorus are likely just because I can't hear them. When I do finally hear them, it is obvious that they are older nestlings. A few nestlings were heard on 5/17, and with most colonies the majority of hatching happens the day after first nestlings are heard, so I estimate that hatching date is ~5/18. The Fledgling dispersal date of pulse 1 is also an estimate as the calls from pulse 2 nestlings make it hard to determine the exact date. For recordings that were analyzed to determine the edge of hatching and dispersal (p1n, p2n) where the two pulaes overlapped I have marked the YNC with the tag YNC-p2 and the older nestling calls with ONC-p1 to distinguish between the two pulses of nestlings. There was also a rain storm on that day which maybe explains the lull. The ARU didn't pick up the colony very well and all vocalizations are quite faint. Female Chatter is never heard, but there is almost continuous Male Chorus, and I can barely hear the young. Fledgling Begging Calls, being more strident, were picked up by the ARUs, and analysis of the Fledgling Begging Calls suggests there were two successful bouts of breeding, with the first bout starting with a small group which then had a larger Addition. This lead to the presence of Fledling Begging Calls from 1-May to 6-May (weak first bout), 22-May to 5-Jun (stronger Addition), and 21-Jun tp 24-Jun (Repeat). If this is correct, I can estimate the breeding stages as Bout #1: Incubation started ~6-Apr, Brooding ~16-Apr, and confirmed to have Fledged on 1-May and Dispersed 6-May. There was an addition to this first bout, with this addition starting to Incubate ~28-Apr, Brooding ~8-May, and was confirmed to have Fledged on 22-May and these fledglings hung around until 5-Jun. Once this first bout was completed, a Repeat bout was initiated and Incubation began ~27-May, Brooding ~7-Jun, and Fledging on 21-Jun and stuck around until 24-Jun, after which the majority of the Fledgling Begging Calls cease. There is a long tail of occasional Fledgling Begging Calls that extends through 27-Jul. I do not know if these are stragglers finishing up a really late breeding attempt, or if these are just fledglings that are re-visiting the area occasionally. Mini Manual was completed.

There were a total of 3 breeding attempts. An initial breeding attempt was identified in April based on the temporal sequence of Male Chorus followed by Female Chatter. 

A second period of Male Chrous and Female Chatter began approximately 14 days later, a separation shorter than the minimum ~30-day interval between breeding attempts in Tricolored Blackbirds, indicating the arrival of an additional cohort and classification of this event as an Addition, this Addition of birds was closer to the other ARU and is not documented here and is documented at the other ARU.

A third period of Male Chorus followed by Female Chatter occurred approximately 30 days after the onset of the initial breeding attempt, consistent with a second breeding attempt by the original cohort. All breeding attempts were classified as Successful based on the presence of Fledgling Begging Calls.

This combination of Additions and Sequential breeding attempts resulted in extended overlap of breeding stages and near-continuous detections of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls from 10 May through ARU retrieval on 18 June. Accordingly, this colony was classified as Complex.
column81: This colony had a Complex form of breeding and exhibited both Sub-colony Addition and Replacement forms. After the first bout of breeding commenced Brooding, there was a Sub-colony Addition on 4-May. These new arrivals would have occupied new nesting sites, as the original individuals that formed the colony were still brooding, and thus nests were occupied. In addition, there was a third bout of Male Chorus that occurs approximately at the time the first Fledgling Begging Calls are heard, that suggest that this is a Replacement bout of breeding where the nesting sites previously occupied are reused for another bout of breeding. This Replacement bout is much smaller than the original bout of breeding, and there are only a handful of Female Chatter in June, and only a few Hatchling Begging Calls in June as well. This second weak bout might have also shown a replacement for the sub-colony addition, though it was hard to document, as it was obscured by the vocalizations from the overlapping, and much larger bout of breeding from the first bout, but the presence of Fledgling Begging Calls into mid-June imply that this Replacement bout of at the orignal nesting sites, was also successful. Additionally, there is evidence that there was a Replacement bout of breeding at the Sub-colony Addition sites in that there are hatchlings heard on June 13, which is 28 days after the hatchlings from the first subcolony addition are heard. column79:
Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were present at the start of the deployment, indicating that a breeding attempt had progressed to fledging prior to installation of the ARU. Following dispersal of fledglings from this initial attempt, a second breeding attempt occurred, evidenced by a temporally distinct cluster of Fledgling Begging Call detections later in the deployment. The clear temporal separation between these two fledging periods supports classification of this colony as Sequential.
During manual review of recordings associated with the second breeding attempt, Nestling Begging Calls were detected, but Hatchling Begging Calls were infrequent and did not reach the daily detection threshold. As a result, the estimated onset of brooding for this attempt is approximate and is denoted with a “~” in Table 5.
The ARI score for the second breeding attempt was zero due to the lack of Nestling Begging Call detections, a pattern that would typically indicate Abandonment. However, the presence of Fledgling Begging Call detections supports classification of this attempt as Partially Abandoned. In-person visits corroborated this interpretation and documented deterioration of the nesting substrate (milk thistle), which had become desiccated and structurally unstable and may have contributed to partial failure of the attempt. Because fledgling production was limited, Fledgling Begging Call detections were sparse and did not meet the daily threshold; consequently, fledging dates are reported as approximate and indicated with a “~” in Table 5.

column79:
Early-season activity was characterized by sustained Male Chorus detections throughout March and April, followed by fewer Female Chatter detections. Vocal detections declined abruptly on 25 April, shortly after the onset of incubation. The ARI score for this breeding attempt was 0.00 due to the absence of Nestling Begging Call detections, a pattern that would ordinarily indicate Abandonment; however, a small fraction of recordings contained Fledgling Begging Call detections, supporting classification as Partially Abandoned. An in-person site visit on 29 April corroborated this classification.
During this period, two sources of disturbance were documented. Feral pig vocalizations were detected in eleven recordings between 24 March and 1 April, and site visits confirmed their presence in the nesting substrate; pigs were removed by 15 April. Coyote vocalizations were detected in five recordings between 29 March and 7 May, and site visits documented their presence near the colony from 29 April to 24 June. Although these disturbances may have contributed to the Partial Abandonment of the first breeding attempt, Male Chorus and Female Chatter detections persisted during the period of pig activity, and the Partial Abandonment occurred approximately ten days after pig removal, suggesting that feral pigs alone were not the primary driver. It is possible that access paths created in the nesting substrate facilitated predator access to nests. Due to the Partial Abandonment, detections of Fledgling Begging Calls were sparse and did not meet the daily threshold, and while there is evidence to support reporting a few successful fledglings, there are not enough detections to determine dates of onset or dispersal.
A second breeding attempt was initiated later in the season and progressed through fledging. A marked increase in Fledgling Begging Call detections on 21 June likely corresponds to the fledging date for this second attempt, which was classified as Successful.
column80:
Early-season activity is high, with strong Male Chorus throughout March and April. Activity drops abruptly on 25 April. A weak bout of Female Chatter in late April indicates that although most birds abandoned, a small number of females remained and nested. A site visit on 29 April confirmed Partial Abandonment: only ~50 birds remained from the original ~500, and only a few females were carrying food. Hatchling and Nestling Begging Calls were not detected for this first attempt, but sparse Fledgling Begging Calls in late May–mid June indicate that a small number of nests succeeded, but the overall pattern is consistent with Partial Abandonment.

A second Retry attempt initiated later in the season and proceeded normally. It was successful. The marked increase in Fledgling Begging Calls on 21 June most likely represents the fledging date for the Retry attempt. 

During this period, two sources of disturbance were documented:
• Feral pigs entered the nesting substrate, with eleven recordings of feral pig vocalizations between 24 March and 1 April and their presence was noted on 1 Apr during a site visit.
• Coyotes were present and may have used pig-created access paths; five recordings with coyote vocalizations were detected between 29 March and 7 May and site visits noted their presence near the colony from 29 Apr to 24 Jun.

Although these disturbances could have contributed to the colony's Partial Abandonment of its first breeding attempt, strong Male Chorus continued throughout the period when feral pigs were active, suggesting that feral pigs alone were not the primary driver of abandonment, and coyotes were present throughout the second successful breeding attempt.

The dominant detection pattern was consistent with a Simple synchronous breeding attempt. However, a small subset of recordings containing Female Chatter after the onset of Brooding, together with extended detections of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls, suggests the presence of limited asynchronous nesting within the colony. Because the overall detection pattern indicates that most nesting activity followed a synchronous trajectory, the colony was classified as Simple.

Also definately some asynchrony - for example :https://arbimon.org/project/tricolored-blackbird-breeding-phenology/visualizer/rec/202905009?a=box,46.88,375,47.2747,21656 has both a fledgling and a young nestling.

column79:
Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections were present in the earliest recordings, indicating that breeding had begun prior to ARU deployment. Continued overlap of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections supports classification of this colony as Asynchronous. The algorithm detected a stronger block of Fledgling Begging Calls starting 5/27, suggesting a second pulse of breeding is embedded in the Asynchronous breeding, however there is not a block of Male Chorus, Female Chatter, Hatchling, or Nestling Begging calls associated with it. A review of recordings around the expected onset of Brooding also failed to locate any Hatchling Begging Calls. This could be due to the Asynchronous nature of the first pulse overlapping the second pulse that this block of Fledgling Begging Calls may represent. Therefore the theoretical second bout of breeding dates for Incubation Onset, and Breeding Onset are inferred from this block of Fledgling Begging Calls which is indicated with a "~".

column79: Two distinct breeding attempts were found, characterized by extended Female Chatter detections and overlapping Begging Call detections, indicating Asynchronous nesting within each attempt. The resulting prolonged presence of Fledgling Begging Call detections reflects overlap between attempts. Both breeding attempts progressed through fledging and dispersal and were classified as Successful.
